factors.title: Restrictions change access to stores
factors.short: PSBB began 10 April 2020 in Jakarta; essential retail was exempted.
factors.evidence: Jakarta announced PSBB from 10 April 2020 for an initial 14 days, extendable. Food, daily-needs retail, and logistics were among the sectors permitted to operate.
factors.scope: Jakarta stores, especially locations dependent on mall visits; grocery and distribution operations.
factors.implication: Movement restrictions can reduce accessible footfall even when grocery operations may continue. Exposure depends on each store’s location and access.
factors.response: Compare affected stores’ footfall and cash contribution; test pickup or delivery where fulfillment costs are justified.
factors.limit: A dated regional policy, not a nationwide blanket store closure or a permanent rule through 2025. Its effect on each MPPA site is not quantified here.
factors.aqcd: Actionable and geographically specific; dates and initial duration are known. No before/after MPPA footfall series is available.

factors.title: Household spending moved into contraction
factors.short: Real household-consumption growth: +5.04% in 2019 versus −2.63% in 2020.
factors.evidence: Indonesia’s real household-consumption growth changed from +5.04% in 2019 to −2.63% in 2020, a decline of 7.67 percentage points.
factors.scope: Indonesian household demand across MPPA formats; premium and discretionary baskets may face different pressure.
factors.implication: Weaker demand makes assumptions about basket size, price sensitivity, and sales recovery more consequential. Format-level sensitivity still needs testing.
factors.response: Stress-test sales and margins under slower recovery; compare affordable essentials with premium and discretionary assortments.
factors.limit: Growth rates describe national real consumption, not MPPA sales, nominal grocery revenue, or the spending level falling by 7.67%.
factors.aqcd: Quantitative and comparable across years. National evidence is mapped to formats; it does not measure each format’s demand.

factors.title: Indonesian respondents changed online shopping activity
factors.short: BPS survey, 2020: 31% reported more online shopping, 28% less, and 41% unchanged.
factors.evidence: In BPS’s 2020 respondent survey, 31% reported increased online shopping during COVID-19, 28% decreased, and the remaining 41% were unchanged.
factors.scope: Indonesian survey respondents; useful for testing online ordering and physical-store access across MPPA formats.
factors.implication: Shopping behavior was mixed. A segment increased online activity, while others reduced it or stayed unchanged; a uniform shift should not be assumed.
factors.response: Test online ordering and pickup with defined customer groups; compare repeat orders, basket values, and contribution after fulfillment costs.
factors.limit: Voluntary online survey using non-probability sampling, not a representative population estimate. These are respondent shares, not sales-growth rates or measured MPPA customer behavior.
factors.aqcd: Quantitative comparison of reported behavior categories. Before-pandemic levels and MPPA-format results were not measured; divisional relevance is an application to test.
factors.chartTitle: Online shopping behavior among BPS respondents

factors.title: Digital payment acceptance expanded
factors.short: QRIS merchants: 5.8 million at end-2020 versus over 12 million by 1 November 2021.
factors.evidence: Bank Indonesia reported 5.8 million QRIS merchants at end-2020 and more than 12 million by 1 November 2021: acceptance more than doubled.
factors.scope: Physical checkout across MPPA formats and the surrounding merchant ecosystem in Indonesia.
factors.implication: Wider acceptance can make digital checkout more familiar while helping smaller rivals offer similar convenience.
factors.response: Audit payment acceptance, transaction failures, fees, and reconciliation; test whether checkout improvements create measurable customer value.
factors.limit: Merchant registrations do not measure grocery demand, unique consumers, transaction profitability, or MPPA’s current payment capability.
factors.aqcd: Dated, quantitative adoption comparison. National infrastructure is relevant to formats, but MPPA’s incremental benefit is not quantified.
factors.unit: Million merchants · later value is a lower bound

factors.title: Jakarta introduced a shopping-bag obligation
factors.short: Governor Regulation 142/2019 was enforced from 1 July 2020 in Jakarta retail locations.
factors.evidence: From 1 July 2020, Jakarta enforced Governor Regulation 142/2019 on environmentally friendly shopping bags in malls, supermarkets, and traditional markets.
factors.scope: MPPA stores within DKI Jakarta and their checkout operations; other locations require separate rule checks.
factors.implication: Bag procurement, checkout processes, and customer communication need to fit the local obligation.
factors.response: Check Jakarta store compliance and suppliers; assess bag availability and customer communication without treating the rule as a nationwide requirement.
factors.limit: The requirement is Jakarta-specific. Available evidence does not establish MPPA’s compliance costs or the rule’s effect on sales.
factors.aqcd: A dated change in obligations with a clear location. Compliance cost and sales impact are not quantified.

factors.title: Food loss and waste expose a resource risk
factors.short: Bappenas estimated 23–48 million tonnes of food loss and waste annually across 2000–2019.
factors.evidence: A Bappenas study released in 2021 estimated national food loss and waste at 23–48 million tonnes per year during 2000–2019.
factors.scope: Fresh-food sourcing, storage, and replenishment in Hypermart, Foodmart, Primo, and Hyfresh.
factors.implication: Perishable assortments are exposed to resource loss. MPPA’s actual shrinkage, disposal costs, and savings potential require company data.
factors.response: Measure waste by category and store; test forecasting, cold-chain controls, and markdowns against their implementation costs.
factors.limit: The range covers the national food chain over two decades. It is neither MPPA’s waste nor a 2020 point estimate, and does not establish a new annual trend.
factors.aqcd: Quantitative context and a specific operational exposure. No comparable MPPA waste series is available, so AQCD coverage is incomplete.
